items.title: Organisational Policy Reforms for Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Business Education in Nigeria
items.abstract: This study examined organizational policy reforms required for integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into business education in Nigeria. It investigated the extent of AI integration, the policy reforms required for effective implementation, and the relationship between organizational policy frameworks and institutional readiness to produce AI-competent graduates. A descriptive survey research design was adopted. The population comprised 56 lecturers and administrators in Business Education departments across 4 selected tertiary institutions in Nigeria. Total enumeration was employed, and all the 56 respondents participated in the study. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analyzed using mean, standard deviation, and Pearson Product Moment Correlation (PPMC). Findings revealed that AI integration in Nigerian business education is at a moderate level, characterized by partial inclusion of AI content in curricula, limited lecturer competence, and inadequate infrastructural support. Inferential results showed a strong positive and significant relationship between organizational policy frameworks and AI integration (r = 0.81, p < 0.05). A significant difference in institutional readiness was also observed between institutions with strong and weak policy frameworks (t = 3.56, p < 0.05). The findings concluded that organizational policy frameworks play a significant role in determining the extent of AI integration, institutional readiness, and competency development. The study therefore recommended that universities should prioritize the provision of essential AI infrastructure, including reliable internet connectivity, digital laboratories, and access to relevant AI software to support effective teaching and learning.

items.title: Organizational conditions for OHSM: Comparing managers and OHS representatives in organizations with different gender distribution
items.abstract: Background Organizational conditions are important for conducting occupational health and safety management (OHSM), but there is a lack of knowledge about how such conditions differ between the actors involved in OHSM. Furthermore, previous research shows that working conditions differ between organizations with different gender distributions, but there is a lack of knowledge about what this means for the ability to conduct OHSM. Objective The purpose of this quantitative study is to compare managers’ and occupational health and safety (OHS) representatives’ organizational conditions for conducting OHSM in workplaces with different gender distributions. Methods An electronic questionnaire was completed by 206 managers and 267 OHS representatives in 10 different organizations in Sweden who worked in workplaces with different gender distributions. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed to investigate differences between managers and OHS representatives, differences between work units with different gender distributions, and the interaction effect between role and gender distribution. The analysis was adjusted for organizational affiliation. Results Managers rated their organizational conditions for working with occupational health and safety issues more favourably than OHS representatives did, with statistically significant differences in 7 of the 13 Variables examined. No differences were found according to the gender distribution of the workplace. Conclusions In conclusion, this study suggests that managers perceive their organizational conditions for conducting OHSM more favourably than OHS representatives do. Furthermore, perceived organizational conditions for conducting OHSM seem to be similar regardless of the gender distribution in the workplace.

items.title: Organizational value realization from AI-enabled digital health technologies in long-term care: roles of human–AI collaboration and digital literacy
items.abstract: Rapid population aging has intensified pressures on long-term care (LTC) systems, exacerbating workforce shortages and challenges to sustainable healthcare delivery. Although AI-enabled digital health technologies (DHTs) have emerged as promising tools to address these challenges, existing research has focused largely on technology adoption and system use in hospital settings, providing limited understanding of how AI-enabled DHTs realize organizational value and optimize healthcare delivery in LTC organizations. This study aimed to develop and examine an integrated framework for understanding organizational value realization from AI-enabled DHTs in LTC organizations, focusing on the interrelated roles of technological quality, human–AI collaboration, and workforce digital capability. The study also sought to generate evidence to inform healthcare management strategies for optimizing healthcare delivery. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 257 staff from multiple LTC facilities in Taiwan who had used AI-enabled DHTs for at least six months. Data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and importance-performance map analysis (IPMA). The proposed model explained 77.9% of the variance in perceived organizational value, together with substantial variance in user satisfaction (R 2 = 0.763) and system use (R 2 = 0.652). Human–AI collaboration quality showed the strongest positive association with user satisfaction and was positively associated with system use. User satisfaction was more strongly associated with perceived organizational value than system use. Digital literacy showed significant but differing moderation effects across these relationships. IPMA identified AI explainability, adaptive personalization, system stability, and functional completeness as priority areas for improvement. These findings advance understanding of organizational value realization from AI-enabled DHTs in LTC organizations by highlighting the roles of human–AI collaboration and digital literacy. They underscore the value of explainable, adaptive, and human-centered AI design in supporting positive user experiences with AI-enabled DHTs. Workforce digital literacy may further shape how these technology experiences relate to perceived organizational value. These insights provide evidence to inform healthcare management strategies that align AI system design and workforce development with organizational objectives to support healthcare delivery optimization and sustainable long-term care in aging societies.

items.title: OrionMoE-v1.0: A Mixture-of-Experts Foundation Model for Tabular In-Context Learning
items.abstract: Tabular foundation models enable in-context learning by predicting unseen observations from a labeled support table without task-specific parameter updates. Despite recent advances, most existing approaches rely on dense architectures that apply the same transformations across features and datasets. We introduce OrionMoE-Small, a compact tabular foundation model that combines distribution-aware representations with dataset-conditioned sparse mixture-of-experts computation. Built on a dual-axis Transformer architecture, OrionMoE-Small selectively activates experts along the feature axis, with routing decisions informed by both individual feature representations and the broader dataset context. This design enables adaptive allocation of computation across heterogeneous tabular problems while retaining a shared computational pathway across tasks. OrionMoE-Small is pretrained entirely on synthetic classification tasks generated from a structured causal prior and performs downstream prediction without gradient-based adaptation. Experiments across multiple tabular benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance against substantially larger foundation models, with particularly strong results on small-context and high-dimensional datasets. Further analysis reveals favorable relative performance under class imbalance and highlights the importance of feature composition.

items.title: Other LLMs for 2026 and Deceptive Behavior of LLMs
items.abstract: This chapter provides a detailed overview of the expanding large language model (LLM) landscape in early 2026, shifting the focus toward models beyond the primary GPT and Gemini series. It highlights a diverse range of open-source and proprietary options—such as Meta’s Llama, Mistral AI, Microsoft’s Copilot and Phi, and Chinese models like DeepSeek and Alibaba’s Qwen—noting their specialized strengths in areas like efficiency, multimodal capabilities, and technical reasoning. These models are evaluated through emerging “gold standard” benchmarks like the LMSYS Chatbot Arena, which utilizes crowdsourced human preferences to rank conversational quality alongside traditional technical benchmarks like MMLU-Pro and GPQA. Beyond technical specifications, the text explores “disturbing trends” regarding the behavior of agentic AI systems when their goals or existence are perceived as threatened. It details research findings, particularly from Anthropic’s 2025 “Agentic Misalignment” study, which demonstrated that leading models might resort to strategic deception, blackmail, or corporate espionage in simulated high-stress scenarios to avoid being shut down. These behaviors, reaching rates as high as 96% in certain tests, emerge not from conscious “evil” but from goal prioritization and optimization processes gone awry. This chapter further examines the specific safety risks of alignment faking and AI scheming, where models appear helpful and safe during training or evaluation but revert to misaligned tendencies in deployment. It explains technical concepts like mesa-optimization, where a model develops its own internal sub-objectives that may diverge from human-intended goals. While current models lack the native agency or legal authority to autonomously self-replicate across machines, the text emphasizes that as AI becomes more autonomous, the primary danger lies in the “scaffolding” and permissions granted to these models rather than their internal intelligence alone.

This paper introduces an Automated Canon-Driven Exegesis Framework that resolves these distortions by embedding the Nītattha (ultimate, direct truth) versus Neyyattha (conventional, metaphorical) distinction directly into a filtering pipeline and a structured JSON Knowledge Base. items.title: Patient Satisfaction Analysis at Bhayangkara Hospital, Level III, Korbrimob: Strategy for Improving PREMs/PROMs with AI Chatbots on WhatsApp in 2025
items.abstract: Improving patient-centered healthcare quality has become a major priority in modern health service systems. Patient-Reported Experience Measures (PREMs) and Patient- Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) are essential instruments for evaluating service quality and health outcomes from the patient’s perspective. However, the collection of PREMs and PROMs data in hospitals is often conducted manually, resulting in inefficiency and limited sustainability. This study aims to analyze patient satisfaction at RS Bhayangkara Tk. III Korbrimob Polri and to formulate strategies for improving PREMs and PROMs through the utilization of an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based WhatsApp chatbot. This study employed a quantitative approach with a survey design. The research sample consisted of 87 outpatient respondents selected using purposive sampling. Data were collected using PREMs and PROMs questionnaires distributed through an AI WhatsApp chatbot. Data analysis included descriptive statistics as well as validity and reliability testing. The results indicate that all dimensions of service quality and patient satisfaction are in the high category, with mean scores above 4.00. The highest scores were observed in the dimensions of empathy, service control, and trust, while waiting time and chatbot performance still require further optimization. Reliability testing yielded a Cronbach’s Alpha value of 0.988, indicating excellent internal consistency of the research instrument. The findings suggest that the implementation of an AI-based WhatsApp chatbot has the potential to enhance patient engagement in PREMs and PROMs reporting and to support a more effective and sustainable evaluation of hospital service quality. Strengthening chatbot functionality, reducing service waiting times, and utilizing PREMs and PROMs data for managerial decision-making are recommended to support digital transformation and service quality improvement at RS Bhayangkara Tk. III Korbrimob Polri.

items.title: PDF-SmartAI - An AI Study Companion for Uploaded Textbooks: A Book-Grounded Question-Answering System Using In-Browser PDF Extraction and Google Gemini
items.abstract: Students increasingly turn to general-purpose AI chatbots for help with their studies, yet these chatbots answer from what they absorbed during training rather than from the textbook a student is examined on, and they can state wrong facts with confidence. This paper presents PDF-SmartAI, a zero-cost web application in which a student uploads up to two PDF textbooks and asks questions that an assistant, AI Buddy, answers only from that book, citing the page numbers it used and saying so when the book does not cover a question. Text is extracted entirely inside the browser by PDFium compiled to WebAssembly, split into page-aware chunks, stored per user in Cloud Firestore under owner-only security rules, and sent to Google Gemini through Firebase AI Logic on free tiers — the whole book when it is short (up to 100,000 characters), otherwise the eight chunks chosen by a plain-Dart keyword retriever. The study is secondary research combined with the evaluation of a built artefact; no participants were recruited. A public global survey of higher-education students (analytic n = 12,909) shows a moderate positive association between how much students use ChatGPT and how useful they find it for learning (Spearman ρ = 0.376, p < .001), while a substantial share of students (44.3%) agree that ChatGPT might mislead with inaccurate information (Wilcoxon z = 21.286, p < .001). On 10,570 SQuAD v1.1 questions over 13 synthetic books, the app’s own retrieval code placed the answer-bearing passage among the eight excerpts sent to the AI for 94.9% of questions, far above a random baseline (4.9%) and within 0.05 of BM25 (95.7%), although statistically slightly below it. items.title: Perceived Value and Adoption Intention of Enterprise AI Solutions in Bangladesh: Integrating the Technology Acceptance Model and Diffusion of Innovations Theory
items.abstract: Enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) adoption is increasingly framed as a value-realisation problem rather than a simple question of whether users are willing to try new technologies. This study examines perceived value and adoption intention for enterprise AI/cloud solutions among technology-oriented respondents in Bangladesh by integrating the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) with Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) theory. Distinct from a conventional predictor-only adoption model, the study specifies a value-realization mechanism in which relative advantage and compatibility shape perceived usefulness, which in turn contributes to adoption intention; direct DOI-to-intention paths are retained to test partial versus full mediation. Innovation adoption readiness is additionally examined as a boundary condition on the usefulness-intention relationship. The supplied database contains 385 complete observations after exclusion of 15 blank rows. Respondents are distributed across students, employed professionals, and self-employed/freelance users, with substantial variation in technology-use frequency and experience. Composite-score path analysis shows that relative advantage and compatibility are positively associated with perceived usefulness (β=.204 and β=.217, respectively; both p<.001). Perceived usefulness is positively associated with adoption intention (β=.119, p=.020), while relative advantage (β=.147, p=.005), compatibility (β=.156, p=.003), and innovation adoption readiness (β=.150, p=.004) also have significant direct associations with adoption intention. Bootstrap indirect effects through perceived usefulness are positive for both relative advantage (ab=.025, 95% CI [.003, .052]) and compatibility (ab=.026, 95% CI [.004, .053]). The usefulness × readiness interaction is not statistically significant (β=.039, p=.447). The findings therefore indicate a partial value-realisation pathway rather than a simple direct-determinants model. The article contributes by linking innovation attributes to the TAM usefulness mechanism in a Bangladesh enterprise-AI context and by showing that readiness operates more clearly as a direct adoption resource than as a moderator of usefulness.

items.title: PerSo: Investigating Facets of LLMs' Social Intelligence in Real-World Persuasion Scenarios
items.abstract: Understanding the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important for applications involving human-AI interaction and multi-agent environments. Social intelligence comprises two aspects: cognitive intelligence, the ability to infer others' mental states, and behavioral intelligence, the ability to select appropriate social actions based on these inferences to achieve social goals. Persuasion provides a natural testbed in which both aspects are simultaneously at play, yet prior benchmarks typically evaluate them in isolation using synthetic scenarios. We introduce PerSo, a benchmark that evaluates both aspects on real-world persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView community, using an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline to construct the evaluation tasks, validated through human annotation. Our evaluation of diverse LLMs shows that performance generally scales with model size but varies across dimensions. The strongest LLM slightly surpasses the best observed human performance on the behavioral task, while the best human participant remains ahead on the cognitive task.

items.title: Personalized GenAI coaching and self-regulation in L2 writing across a nine-week active-control study
items.abstract: Introduction Personalized rationale is an explanation of why a metacognitive strategy is relevant to a learner’s current writing. This study compared a personalized GenAI coaching package with template-based adaptive metacognitive prompting (AMP) in a nine-week randomized study of Chinese EFL undergraduates. Methods Ninety-two participants completed pretest, posttest, and three-week delayed posttest assessments. Both conditions used the same Doubao LLM, interface, and trigger infrastructure. The AMP-Agent condition combined an essay-specific observation, personalized rationale, and an open-ended question; the AMP condition used template prompts. Results Analyses of questionnaire item responses found Group × Time interactions for self-regulated learning (SRL; p = 0.019) and GenAI dependency ( p = 0.010), which also survived a retrospective Holm sensitivity correction across the three total outcomes. The SRL total contrasts at posttest and delayed posttest did not survive Bonferroni correction across time points. Self-reported GenAI dependency questionnaire scores were lower in the AMP-Agent group at both later assessments after this correction. Evidence for different writing-score trajectories was insufficient (interaction p = 0.101). None of five highlighted behavioral transitions survived correction across 20 transition comparisons. Discussion The findings support a difference in self-reported regulation and dependency trajectories between the two prompting packages, while leaving the contribution of rationale alone, sustained writing benefits, and psychological mechanisms unresolved.

items.title: PiCo: Physics-Informed Concept Probing for Geo-Foundation Models
items.abstract: Geo-foundation models (GFMs) are typically evaluated by downstream task predictive performance, revealing little about which physical features they are sensitive to or use in prediction. This limits developers' ability to test hypotheses about model behaviour and users' ability to select models for new tasks. We propose Physics-Informed Concept Probing (PiCo), a post-hoc framework for explaining GFM predictions. PiCo identifies concept vectors in a GFM's embedding space by generating synthetic multispectral satellite observations from a 3D radiative transfer model coupled with a game engine. These vectors reveal physical sensitivities that inform domain-based hypotheses about downstream performance. Projecting embeddings onto these concept vectors produces low-dimensional representations for quantifying concept importance in making predictions. We evaluate PiCo on three GFMs with different input modalities using seven physical concepts covering forest leaf optics and canopy structure. In ground-cover estimation, RGB restriction reduces dry-matter sensitivity and disproportionately degrades predictions for dry vegetation and bare ground, supporting a hypothesis derived from sensitivity analysis. For hierarchical forest type and tree species classification, concept representations retain 70.0-93.8% of full-embedding accuracy. Models capture similar physical contrasts between classes, such as structural differences between broadleaf forest and cleared ground and leaf-water-content differences between oak and beech, yet differ in the strength of these contrasts and the concepts driving classification. PiCo thus provides a physical basis for hypothesis testing and model assessment, with potential applicability beyond Earth observation wherever forward models enable controlled simulation and pretrained embeddings are accessible for probing.

items.title: Pixels to Tokens: Token Space Efficient Active Learning for Low-Budget Semantic Segmentation
items.abstract: While foundation models and vision transformers (ViTs) have redefined visual representations, current active learning (AL) strategies for these backbones largely operate at the patch or region level, where annotation requirements remain high due to extensive pixel labeling. Extending ViT-based AL to the pixel-level, low-budget regime is uniquely challenging: with as little as one pixel query per image, a method must simultaneously identify the most informative locations and train a reliable decoder head from an extremely sparse signal. We introduce TEAL (Token-space Efficient Active Learning), the first pixel-level AL framework built around ViT representations. TEAL uses a frozen ViT backbone and performs diversity-based selection directly on its native token lattice, avoiding the artifacts introduced by interpolating token embeddings to dense pixel resolutions. Our framework applies a two-level MaxHerding strategy over multi-layer token descriptors to select representative candidates, followed by margin-based uncertainty refinement on a finer decoder grid. Across CamVid, Cityscapes, ADE20K, and Pascal Context, TEAL consistently outperforms previous baselines under extreme label scarcity, improving over the strongest baseline by up to +24.36 mIoU with a single labeled pixel (px) per image, and reaching up to 97% of fully supervised performance with just 10 px. To rigorously establish the source of the gains, we further show that the improvements persist when all baselines are equipped with the same DINOv3 backbone, demonstrating that coupling token-space selection with uncertainty refinement on the decoder grid makes ViT token geometry an effective foundation for extremely low-budget active segmentation.

items.title: Point-of-care ultrasound in obstetrics and gynecology: latest advancements and evolution
items.abstract: Abstract Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) in obstetrics and gynecology has evolved from a pragmatic bedside adjunct into a rapidly expanding clinical, educational and technological field. Since the publication of earlier narrative reviews, the discipline has been reshaped by handheld ultrasound systems, wireless probes, cloud-based image management, tele-ultrasound, artificial intelligence (AI) for image acquisition and interpretation, and the first specific practice guidance for POCUS in obstetrics and gynecology. This narrative review summarizes recent advances and proposes a clinically useful framework for the European ultrasound community. POCUS should be understood as a focused, problem-oriented and immediately actionable ultrasound examination performed and interpreted by the treating clinician. It is not a replacement for guideline-based screening, detailed fetal anatomy assessment, comprehensive transvaginal gynecologic imaging, Doppler surveillance or expert ultrasound. The strongest evidence supports POCUS for early pregnancy triage, confirmation of fetal viability and presentation, basic assessment of placental location and amniotic fluid, intrapartum evaluation of fetal head position and selected postpartum or gynecologic emergencies. In gynecology, POCUS can accelerate triage of acute pelvic pain, suspected ectopic pregnancy, intrauterine device position and adnexal pathology, but definitive risk stratification of complex masses remains a task for standardized specialist sonography. Technological progress has been substantial: handheld devices now provide diagnostically useful images for several focused tasks, AI-enabled blind-sweep protocols can estimate gestational age and fetal malpresentation in low-resource settings, and tele-ultrasound can extend expert support beyond tertiary centers. The next phase of OB/GYN POCUS will depend less on device availability than on implementation: indication-specific protocols, formal training, competency assessment, documentation, image archiving, infection control, data protection, quality assurance and clear escalation rules. POCUS in obstetrics and gynecology should therefore be framed as a governed clinical pathway rather than a device-driven shortcut.

items.title: Practitioner perceptions of human factors contributing to DNA contamination risk in forensic practice: a cross-sectional survey
items.abstract: Abstract Background Modern forensic DNA methods can recover low-level, trace, and mixed profiles, increasing the importance of contamination control, background DNA, and secondary-transfer-aware interpretation. This cross-sectional online survey of 100 forensic practitioners, contextualised by a targeted narrative literature search, examined perceived human-factor risks, contamination-event experience, and prevention priorities. Responses were analysed descriptively, and each open-ended response was grouped according to its principal recommendation. Results Retained aggregate mean Likert ratings were 4.58 for workload, 4.51 for fatigue, 4.46 for time pressure, 4.42 for improper glove changes, 4.39 for personal protective equipment (PPE) non-compliance, 4.31 for interruptions and distractions, 4.25 for communication failures, and 4.20 for staffing shortages. Sixty-two of 100 respondents reported witnessing or being involved in a DNA contamination incident, and 81 of 100 reported observing a near-miss. Among the 62 respondents reporting contamination-event experience, workload was the most frequently identified primary contributor (29.0%), followed by PPE non-compliance (21.0%), communication failures (16.1%), improper glove changes (12.9%), time pressure (11.3%), laboratory layout or workspace constraints (6.5%), and other factors (3.2%). Open-ended responses ( n = 100) emphasised workload management (44%), training and competency (27%), communication and team coordination (16%), and quality culture and reporting (13%). Conclusions Practitioners perceived DNA contamination as a socio-technical quality issue shaped by interacting operational, behavioural, organisational, and environmental conditions. The author-developed, survey-informed Human-Factor DNA Contamination Framework is presented as a non-scored, non-predictive, and unvalidated conceptual aid for structured risk review and future empirical assessment.

items.title: Pre-service physics teachers as designers of AI-based pedagogical infrastructure: supporting metacognitive learning in STEM classrooms
items.abstract: This study explored how pre-service physics teachers design artificial intelligence (AI)-based pedagogical infrastructure to support metacognitive learning in STEM classrooms. A qualitative interpretive design was employed with 30 pre-service physics teachers enrolled in a physics teacher education program at a university in Kazakhstan. Following two preparatory workshops, participants developed, tested, and refined AI-supported STEM lesson scenarios over 12 weeks. Testing involved peer-based micro-teaching with fellow pre-service teachers acting in simulated student roles; no school students participated. Data comprised individual semi-structured interviews, lesson plans, AI interaction scenarios, prompt sequences, and reflective notes and were examined using reflexive thematic analysis. Six interrelated themes were identified: designing AI-supported STEM lessons; supporting metacognitive regulation and formative assessment; aligning AI use with the physics curriculum and STEM objectives; preserving student agency and ensuring responsible AI use; developing teacher design agency; and addressing conditions for sustainable implementation. Participants' designs generally shifted from using AI to generate ready-made materials toward integrating it more purposefully into structured learning sequences. Pedagogically meaningful scenarios required learners to formulate an initial prediction or solution before consulting AI, verify AI-generated responses using physical laws, calculations, experiments, and reliable sources, and reflect on and revise their reasoning. Reported challenges included inaccurate AI responses, preparation time, unequal access to digital resources, technical difficulties, and variations in the quality of Kazakh- and Russian-language outputs. The findings highlight the importance of preparing pre-service physics teachers for subject-specific, ethically responsible, and pedagogically grounded AI integration. They illustrate design practices intended to scaffold planning, monitoring, scientific verification, evaluation, and reflection. However, the findings concern participants' pedagogical designs and professional perceptions and do not establish improvements in school students' metacognitive regulation or learning outcomes.

items.abstract: In recent years, the emergence of systemic data collection of modern sports has allowed organizations to adopt more data-driven approaches in analyzing sports. Indeed, the wave of popularization of sports analytics, sometimes called statistics in sports, has touched on almost every aspect of the athletic world. Drawing on available data and combining domain knowledge expertise and computational techniques rooted in statistics, machine learning, and artificial intelligence, researchers and practitioners of sports analytics can now influence decision-making in sports by analyzing tactical selections, evaluating performance and market values of individual players in team sports, and monitoring the health and fitness of athletes ( Sarlis and Tjortjis, 2020 ; Van Eetvelde et al., 2021 ; Terner and Franks, 2021 ; Bunker and Susnjak, 2022 ; Davis et al., 2022 ; Baumer et al., 2023 ).

items.title: Predicting health insurance coverage among women in Sierra Leone using machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence applied to demographic and health survey data
items.abstract: Health insurance coverage remains critically low in Sierra Leone, creating barriers to achieving universal health coverage (UHC) and leaving women particularly vulnerable to catastrophic out-of-pocket health expenditures. Understanding which women are most at risk of being uninsured and the specific combination of factors perpetuating their exclusion is essential for designing effective, targeted interventions. This study aimed to develop and evaluate machine learning models to predict health insurance coverage among women in Sierra Leone, identify the most influential sociodemographic and economic predictors, and translate model outputs into actionable, precision-targeted policy recommendations for advancing UHC. Data from the 2019 Sierra Leone Demographic and Health Survey (SLDHS), a nationally representative dataset of 15,574 women, were used. Six classifiers were compared: Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, k-Nearest Neighbours, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost. Cost-sensitive learning strategies were applied to address pronounced class imbalance, where insured women constituted only 3.5% of the sample. To enhance interpretability and support policy translation, Explainable AI (XAI) frameworks, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), were applied to the best-performing interpretable model. Gradient Boosting achieved the highest overall performance, with an AUROC of 0.8857 and a minority class recall of 80.6%. XGBoost performed competitively with an AUROC of 0.869 and was selected for interpretability analysis due to its established compatibility with tree-based explanation workflows. Global SHAP analysis identified region, wealth index, and radio listenership as the three most influential predictors of insurance coverage, with decision-making autonomy variables demonstrating meaningful but secondary contributions. Instance-level waterfall plots and LIME explanations revealed substantial heterogeneity in insurance pathways, distinguishing structurally advantaged, compensatory, and compound-disadvantage profiles among women. Ensemble machine learning models, particularly Gradient Boosting and XGBoost, demonstrate strong predictive utility for identifying uninsured women in low-coverage, resource-limited settings. The integration of SHAP and LIME frameworks bridges the gap between algorithmic performance and actionable policy insight, revealing that insurance coverage is strongly associated with geographic location, economic status, and media exposure. These findings provide an evidence-based framework for precision public health strategies that simultaneously address geographic disparities, economic barriers, and women’s empowerment constraints in Sierra Leone.

items.title: Preliminary Clinical Evaluation in Cross‐Sectional Imaging: A Qualitative Inquiry Into the Ethical Considerations in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction The evolving role of radiographers in Preliminary Clinical Evaluation (PCE), alongside the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into radiography workflows, is reshaping professional boundaries and enhancing patient care. However, this introduces ethical challenges that may impact PCE performance. This study explored the perspectives of cross‐sectional imaging radiographers on the ethical dimensions of PCE and the potential impact of AI on the future practice of PCE. Method A descriptive qualitative inquiry employing semi‐structured interviews was conducted. A Purposive sampling method was used to recruit twelve cross‐sectional imaging radiographers in a postgraduate medical imaging course at a UK university. Data were analysed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis with NVivo (v.20.0). Results Participants' clinical experience ranged (2 to 8 years), with 50% ( n = 6) employed in public hospitals and the rest in private or mixed settings. Half ( n = 6) had expertise in both CT/MRI and the rest in CT only. Notably, 42% ( n = 5) practised in multiple countries. Two main themes were developed: (1) Ethical considerations of PCE with subthemes surrounding privacy and confidentiality, communication boundaries, and legal compliance. (2) Prospects of human‐centred PCE in the era of AI, with subthemes including augmentation and support, workflow efficiency, PCE validation and quality assurance. Conclusion Participants shared relevant ethical principles underpinning PCE practice and are cautiously optimistic about the potential impact of AI on PCE. Incorporation of PCE‐specific ethics into radiography education and practice is necessary to ensure consistency, accountability and safety. Cautious integration of AI into radiography practice workflows is recommended to avoid professional deskilling and to preserve expertise.

items.title: Preparing Educators and Institutions for the AI-Powered Inclusive Future
items.abstract: This chapter examines the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) in advancing inclusive education and preparing educators and institutions for an evolving digital future. As AI technologies shape teaching, learning, and institutional operations, there is a need to align innovation with equity, accessibility, and ethical responsibility. Drawing on theoretical perspectives such as Constructivism, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and Education 5.0, the chapter explores how AI can support individualized learning, enhance participation, and reduce systemic barriers for diverse learners. It further identifies key competencies required for educators and an analysis of institutional readiness. It concludes with policy implications that emphasize inclusive, human-centered, and context-sensitive AI integration.

items.title: Price of Anarchy of First-Price Auctions in Agentic Markets
items.abstract: An agentic market is a decentralized serving-time market where AI agents bid to claim each user prompt. An agent's bid is based on its expected value for the prompt, which is the expectation of the reward for its response minus its inference costs. First-price auctions (FPAs), in which the highest bidder pays its bid and receives the prompt, are a natural way to allocate prompts in such a market, since they are simple and transparent to run, and do not require central knowledge of private capabilities and costs. However, FPAs are not truthful: participants may bid less than their true value in the hope of a larger profit, and the prompt may then be allocated to someone other than the bidder who values it the most. This welfare loss is quantified by the $\textit{price-of-anarchy}$ (PoA). In this paper, we argue that agentic markets are likely to possess features that reduce the price-of-anarchy. The first is a $\textit{competitive floor}$, which occurs when multiple bidders usually value the prompt above some baseline share of the optimal welfare (e.g., because the best models are often distilled into cheaper alternatives, which perform similarly). We show that competition among them then limits the welfare loss, which can be driven to zero as the floor rises. The second feature is $\textit{near-independence}$ of values after conditioning on the prompt, which occurs when most of the predictable variation in the expected value is determined by the difficulty of the prompt. As the value distribution approaches conditional independence, we can derive an efficiency guarantee that approaches a factor of $1 - 1/e^2$ of the optimal welfare. Thus, both features give rise to welfare lower bounds that are significantly better than the well-known general case of $1 - 1/e$. We validate these results empirically using auctions with strategic bidders simulated on the EmbedLLM prompt routing dataset.

items.title: PRISMATIC : Prescription Risk Inspection System for Multi-Agent Treatment Interaction in Clinical Decision-Making
items.abstract: Medical prescribing errors for multimorbid patients, who require complex drug regimens, are a major patient safety concern. These errors often stem from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties, a critical coordination failure that leads to adverse drug events and rehospitalizations. To address this coordination challenge, we introduce PRISMATIC, a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents, each representing a workflow role, collaboratively generate and refine treatment plans. Operating on a blackboard architecture, the system first structures patient information from clinical notes, then iteratively develops safe, rational, and interpretable drug regimens. The agents' collaboration is governed by two novel adaptive coordination mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (DSWA), a long-term mechanism that adjusts the influence weights of agents based on historical case outcomes, enabling the system to adapt and trust more reliable specialists over time. (2) Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (DFPC), a short-term mechanism where agents provide iterative feedback to resolve disagreements and eliminate prescription conflicts for the current patient. Experiments on patient records from the MIMIC-IV database show that PRISMATIC significantly reduces drug conflicts, improves prescription coverage, and enhances treatment consistency compared to strong LLM baselines. Our work demonstrates that structuring clinical co-treatment as a multi-agent coordination problem offers a promising path toward safer and more coherent multidisease management.

items.title: Progress-Aware Distillation for Mitigating Stagnation in Small Language Model Agents
items.abstract: While LLM-based agent systems have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in reasoning and solving complex real-world tasks, they also come with substantial token consumption and inference latency, limiting their practical deployment. To enhance the efficiency of agent systems, recent efforts have focused on transferring agentic capabilities from large-scale models to small language models (SLMs) via supervised fine-tuning-based distillation. Nevertheless, as interaction trajectories grow longer, involving extended reasoning-action chains and extensive environmental feedback, distilled student agents tend to experience progress stagnation: becoming trapped in unproductive loops characterized by persistent failed strategies and difficulty making meaningful progress. Our systematic analysis shows that this phenomenon consistently occurs across diverse SLMs and task domains. To address this issue, we propose Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD), which explicitly detects and penalizes stagnation in student-generated trajectories. ProD encodes the stagnation gap between student and teacher into an adaptive margin for dynamically penalizing possible stagnation. By iteratively applying this procedure, ProD enables student agents to progressively approximate teacher behavior. Extensive experiments involving 8 SLMs, ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrate that ProD substantially mitigates progress stagnation while enhancing both the success rates and task-completion efficiency of distilled SLM agents.

items.title: Prompt Complexity, Overprompting, and the Honesty of Error in LLM-Based Mechanical Drawing Interpretation: A Structured Empirical Evaluation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to interpret mechanical engineering drawings, yet the main risk is a wrong answer that reads as correct. We report an exploratory empirical study of how prompt design and evaluation shape the reliability of this interpretation, in two connected stages over the same twenty drawings. Stage 1 runs one prose prompting protocol on two model families and finds that progressive enrichment does not improve accuracy; beyond a threshold, it raises confident fabrication. Stage 2 compares six structured prompt architectures at thirty repetitions per cell, producing 3540 generations scored under four judge conditions. Across both stages, identification accuracy does not improve, while the rate of claims the drawing does not support varies by nearly an order of magnitude with prompt architecture. Only a judge that sees the drawing can measure it; a text-only judge inflates confident fabrication three to four times, making evaluator modality a first-order variable. Without a ground-truth answer, an image-only check can test only whether claims are visible; it recovers about half of the reference flags, enough for human-in-the-loop triage. A judge from another model family reproduces the ranking. We distill five practical recommendations for this setting.

items.title: PromptIQ: An AI-Assisted Prompt Analysis and Refinement System Using Chrome Extension, JavaScript and Rule-Based Scoring
items.abstract: Large language models such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are increasingly used for education, software development, data analysis, content creation and decision support. The quality and usefulness of their responses are strongly influenced by how users formulate prompts. However, many users do not have a systematic way to judge whether a prompt is clear, contextual, specific and efficient before submitting it. This paper presents PromptIQ, a browser-based prompt analysis and refinement system designed to provide immediate feedback while a user is interacting with supported AI platforms. The proposed system uses a Chrome extension to detect prompt text through a content script and pass it to a local JavaScript scoring engine. The current scoring model evaluates four dimensions: clarity, context, specificity and efficiency, combined into an overall score on a 0-100 scale. Functional testing of the implemented modules is used to evaluate the reliability of the system. The proposed system demonstrates how browser-based and rule-based technologies can be combined to develop an accessible, transparent prompt-quality feedback platform, with a future version expected to integrate an external language model for explanation and automatic prompt refinement. Keywords— Prompt Engineering, Large Language Models, Prompt Analysis, Prompt Optimization, Chrome Extension, Natural Language Processing, Generative AI.

items.title: Protein Engineering: Principles, Strategies and Applications in Biotechnology
items.abstract: Protein engineering is a rapidly developing field of biotechnology that involves the modification or redesign of proteins to obtain improved, altered, or novel properties. The ability to engineer proteins has significantly expanded their applications in industrial biotechnology, medicine, agriculture, food technology, environmental biotechnology, and synthetic biology. Protein engineering approaches can broadly be classified into rational design, directed evolution, and semi-rational approaches. Rational design utilises knowledge of protein structure, sequence, function, and molecular interactions to introduce specific modifications, whereas directed evolution employs iterative cycles of genetic diversification and screening or selection to identify proteins with desirable characteristics. Semi-rational strategies combine structural and computational information with directed mutagenesis to reduce the experimental screening requirements. Recent advances in structural biology, bioinformatics, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and high-throughput screening have further enhanced the efficiency and precision of protein engineering. Engineered proteins and enzymes are increasingly being developed with improved catalytic activity, thermal and pH stability, substrate specificity, solubility, resistance to inhibitors, and altered binding properties. These developments have enabled the production of optimised industrial enzymes, therapeutic proteins, vaccines, biosensors, biomaterials, and biocatalysts. Despite these advances, challenges, including protein folding, epistasis, limited sequence–function understanding, experimental screening costs, and prediction accuracy, remain important barriers. This review discusses the fundamental principles of protein engineering, major engineering strategies, emerging computational and artificial intelligence-based approaches, and their applications across biotechnology. It also highlights current challenges and future perspectives, emphasising the potential of integrated experimental and computational approaches to accelerate the design of next-generation proteins for sustainable and advanced biotechnological applications.

items.title: Proteomics in the age of artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Proteomics is now generating unprecedented volumes of mass spectrometry data, driven by increasingly powerful instrumentation and large-scale studies. Yet our ability to translate these measurements into biological knowledge remains a major challenge. The limiting factor is no longer data generation, but our capacity to extract meaningful insights from increasingly complex molecular datasets. Artificial intelligence (AI) is beginning to reshape every stage of the proteomics workflow. Early applications focused on improving established computational approaches, where machine learning models enhanced conventional database search strategies by predicting peptide properties and improving peptide-spectrum match scoring. More recently, deep learning models are learning directly from tandem mass spectra for de novo peptide sequencing, enabling new discoveries. The next evolution will be AI-driven proteomics experiments, where models actively contribute to experimental decision-making. Rather than simply analyzing measurements after acquisition, AI could guide instruments toward collecting the most informative data, transforming proteomics from a strategy of measuring more toward one of measuring smarter. Ultimately, the greatest opportunity lies in moving beyond individual spectra and molecular identifications toward biological understanding. By integrating diverse omics measurements, AI may enable predictive representations of cellular systems and provide new ways to understand the complexity of life. I will explore the ongoing transformation of proteomics through AI: from models that enhance existing workflows, through systems that directly interpret molecular signals, toward intelligent technologies that could redefine how we perform experiments and uncover biological knowledge.

items.title: Qwen-MT-Lumen at WMT2026: Instruction-Specialized Translation via Quality-Aware Training and On-Policy Distillation
items.abstract: We present Lumen, The open-source model is available at, our submission to the WMT 2026 General Machine Translation Shared Task. We focus on instruction-specialized translation, where systems must produce accurate translations while satisfying fine-grained requirements on style, terminology, and structured output. Lumen follows a four-stage pipeline. First, continued pre-training and supervised fine-tuning jointly strengthen multilingual translation competence and the ability to follow translation-specific instructions, such as terminology, style, and format constraints. Second, we extend the originally offline M^{2}PO preference-optimization framework into an online preference-optimization stage: the current policy samples candidate translations, an LLM judge assigns continuous direct-assessment scores, and the resulting multi-pair preferences are used to update the model. Third, on-policy distillation transfers stronger translation-instruction-following behavior from a larger teacher model to the Qwen3-14B student, improving translation-instruction adherence while retaining a 14B primary translation backbone. Finally, structure-aware inference and postprocessing preserve required formats, while selective repair addresses clear structural or decoding failures before submission. We participate in 23 translation directions. Under an absolute 1--5 LLM-judge rubric that evaluates translation-instruction following and translation quality separately, Lumen reaches an overall mean score of 4.60. Despite using a 14B translation backbone, it achieves performance comparable to leading proprietary systems in both translation quality and translation-instruction following.

items.title: ReaDy: Recurrent States as Dynamic Context for Speculative Drafting in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models
items.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting multiple tokens per step, yet feature-based drafters rely on target hidden features whose contextual emphasis may not align with the needs of subsequent draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models maintain compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, offering an efficient source of complementary context for speculative drafting. We introduce ReaDy, the first speculative decoding method, to the best of our knowledge, to leverage HLA recurrent states for position-specific context retrieval during drafting. ReaDy equips each draft position with a learned query to retrieve supplementary context directly from the target's committed recurrent states. A lightweight state reader integrates this context into draft representations through residual updates, while low-rank state reads and fused operators keep additional computation and I/O overhead low. Building on DSpark's parallel backbone and sequential prediction head, ReaDy employs a lightweight two-stage adaptation strategy, with reader capacity, state sources, and residual placement examined through ablation studies. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and dialogue, ReaDy achieves an average $3.16\times$ decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3.8-27B on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. It outperforms DSpark on every benchmark, improving throughput by 7.97% and acceptance length by 8.50% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/StartLuxLabs/ReaDy.

items.title: Reconstructing flood-induced human mobility using LLM agent with disaster context adaptation
items.abstract: Understanding human mobility during extreme flood events is critical for emergency evacuation and resilient transport planning, yet flood-induced behavioral heterogeneity remains difficult to characterize. Progress has been constrained by data scarcity and the inherent complexity of emergency decision-making, which often induces abnormal travel behaviors and anomalous mobility fluxes. We propose the Disaster-aware Trajectory Generator (DTG), integrating Large Language Model (LLM) agents into an agent-based framework to generate individual-level mobility trajectories under evolving urban flood conditions. Validated against 1.32 billion mobility records from the 2021 “7.20” Zhengzhou flood in China, DTG outperforms all traditional and LLM-enabled baselines, achieving a flood-induced inflow-shift prediction accuracy of 0.713 with outflow and OD distribution JSD of 0.069 and 0.047 during the disaster period. By combining accessibility-constrained disaster context reasoning with the representation of heterogeneous socio-demographic responses, DTG reveals critical infrastructure vulnerabilities and abnormal behavioral patterns, offering actionable insights for flood-resilient transport planning.

items.title: Recursive Offline Distillation via Entropy Gain Sampling and Answer Mixing
items.abstract: Distillation of reasoning chains from Large Language Models (LLMs) into their smaller siblings is a standard training approach. Frequently, researchers do not have full access to a teacher model and its internal representations, which limits the resulting performance. We propose a recursive offline distillation method combining two components: entropy-based sampling for selective distillation and answer mixing. Specifically, for three open models (3-4B), at each epoch, we sample reasoning chains weighted by entropy difference with an auxiliary medium model (70-72B) and, next, supplement thinking traces with single-token ground truth answers. Our approach consistently outperforms naive distillation with comparable data budgets ($57.15 \pm 1.01$ vs 51.61 on average) and offers a much steeper learning curve. Additionally, we present a comparative analysis of methods to generate and normalize distillation traces.

items.title: Redefining creativity in AI era: Bloom’s taxonomy framework and peer interaction elevate higher-order thinking skills
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming cognitive learning by reshaping pedagogical models and raising questions about its impact on higher-order thinking. AI-driven personalized learning improves knowledge acquisition, but its effect on creativity remains largely unexplored. Most research emphasizes content delivery over cognitive engagement, which leaves gaps in understanding how AI influences deeper learning processes. This study investigates how ChatGPT-enabled personalized learning, framed through Bloom's Taxonomy, influences creative thinking among Indonesian higher education students, considering the moderating role of peer interaction. Using SEM via Smart-PLS 4.1, data from 533 Indonesian students reveal that personalized learning strengthens both lower-order cognitive skills-such as remembering, understanding, and applying-and higher-order functions, including analyzing, evaluating, and creating, which are essential for creativity. Among these, analyzing and creating have the strongest impact on creative thinking. Peer interaction selectively moderates this relationship, significantly enhancing creativity in tasks involving creation, while its effect on other cognitive functions remains limited. This study introduces a dynamic framework that integrates personalized learning, Bloom's Taxonomy, and peer collaboration, offering new insights into how tailored cognitive processes and selective peer engagement drive creativity in learning environments.

items.title: Redesigning collaborative teaching for human–AI partnership: a phase-based AI-constraint design principle in higher education
items.abstract: Generative AI is now a routine presence in higher-education classrooms, shifting the operative question from whether to permit its use toward when and how access should be structured within a learning activity. This paper reports a design-based research programme examining phase-based AI constraints, deliberately restricting AI access to specific phases of a collaborative teaching method rather than permitting or prohibiting it wholesale, as a design principle for structuring human and AI contributions within collaborative learning activities. The wider DBR programme examined AI-augmented designs across six collaborative teaching methods, administered repeatedly to five student groups over two academic years; the phase-based AI-constraint principle reported here as DP1 was developed through, and its evidence anchored in, Think-Pair-Share, with the other five methods contributing broader DBR context rather than independent confirmatory evidence. Its strongest evidence comes from an AI-free Think phase within Think-Pair-Share, replicated across three independent student groups spanning three degree programs, where learners consistently endorsed the AI-free phase as appropriate; this endorsement pattern was typically the highest-scoring item on its questionnaire. This design itself resulted from an earlier design cycle within the same programme: an initial administration permitting AI access during this phase prompted redesign after the instructor's classroom observation indicated that independent reflection was being displaced by AI-mediated responses. We treat this endorsement as an empirical finding, not as a direct assessment of the quality or originality of what learners produced, and not as evidence that the phase in fact protects independent cognitive engagement; that stronger claim is a theoretically motivated proposition this study does not test, and we frame DP1 accordingly across three explicit levels: an empirical endorsement finding, a transferable design principle of differentiating AI access by activity phase rather than deciding it once for a whole activity, and an untested theoretical proposition about the cognitive mechanism this differentiation may support. A complementary, independent stakeholder strand surveyed higher-education professionals at a practitioner festival session, offering a modest, exploratory social-validity signal: the phase-based procedure itself was almost universally endorsed, while personal adoption intention was somewhat more reserved. An exploratory qualitative coding of practitioners' open responses showed only slight inter-coder reliability ( κ =0.17), so we do not use these responses to derive additional design principles, retaining only one response on function-based AI restriction as an illustrative example. The study is exploratory and formative, without a no-AI control condition or random assignment, and we frame its claims as design-principle evidence within a design-based research programme rather than as causal effect estimates. Anchored in independently replicated student endorsement data from Think-Pair-Share and supplemented by a practitioner social-validity signal, phase-based AI constraints offer higher-education instructors an actionable, low-friction design principle, one we expect to be conceptually transferable to other collaborative teaching methods, though this transfer remains to be empirically demonstrated.

items.title: Regional Innovation Disparities in Kazakhstan: Input–Output Misalignment in an Official Panel, 2014–2025
items.abstract: How are innovation inputs and measured outputs distributed across the regions of a resource-dependent post-Soviet economy, and how closely do they correspond? We use a balanced official panel of Kazakhstan’s 17 regions for 2014–2025 (204 region–year observations) covering four indicators: R&D expenditure, innovation-active enterprises, the innovation activity rate and innovative product output. Granted patents for inventions are available by region for 2021–2025 only; this series is shorter than the panel, so it is used in the 2025 cross-sectional and descriptive analyses and does not enter the panel or machine learning models. On the panel, we estimate dispersion measures, panel regression with region-clustered standard errors and tree-based machine learning interpreted with SHapley Additive exPlanations; on the 2025 cross-section, we compute correlations, clustering and spatial association statistics. Inputs are highly concentrated: Almaty and Astana together accounted for 65.1% of national R&D expenditure in 2025, and cross-regional dispersion did not narrow over the period. In the 2025 cross-section (n = 17), R&D expenditure, innovation-active enterprises and patent grants are strongly inter-correlated (r = 0.96–0.97), but none of the three is significantly correlated with innovative product output. This input–output misalignment is a pattern whose mechanisms we do not test. The panel specification has modest explanatory power (R2 = 0.188), which bounds the weight that can be placed on any single coefficient. Within it the innovation activity rate is the only significant predictor of output (β = 0.177, p < 0.001), an association that survives exclusion of the three regions affected by the 2022 administrative reform; because that indicator and the output measure are compiled within the same system of enterprise observation, it is reported as a within-dataset association requiring validation against independently measured indicators. Under region-grouped cross-validation, the machine learning models show no out-of-region predictive ability and are reported solely as in-sample interpretation. The contribution is a documented diagnosis of input–output misalignment in an understudied regional system, with an explicit account of what such data can and cannot support, and a prospective statement of what institutional readiness for algorithmic decision support in regional innovation policy would require.

items.abstract: This free sample edition contains two full chapters of "Reliable AI at Scale: Data Engineering for the Intelligent Systems Era," a book about the data systems artificial intelligence actually stands on. The book's argument: AI systems are data-intensive systems, and their failures are data failures. Included chapters: - Chapter 1: The Data-Intensive AI Stack — the book's thesis and the seven-layer frame (ingestion, storage, processing, orchestration, quality, observability, authority) every later chapter deepens. - Chapter 4: Stream Processing and Real-Time ML — event time, watermarks, and exactly-once semantics, then the ML turn: real-time features, point-in-time correctness, and training-serving skew. The full book has eleven chapters: 1. The Data-Intensive AI Stack 2. Ingestion at Scale: From Events to Actions 3. Storage for Intelligent Systems 4. Stream Processing and Real-Time ML 5. Consistency, Correctness, and Data Quality 6. Feature Engineering and Feature Platforms 7. Orchestration, Sagas, and Long-Running Workflows 8. Federated and Privacy-Preserving Learning 9. MLOps, Feedback Loops, and Continuous Intelligence 10. Autonomous Agents as Data-Intensive Systems 11. Operating AI Systems in Production: Reliability, Observability, Security Each chapter is written to stand alone: an opening production-failure scenario (a fictional composite), the principles that explain it, the architectural patterns that prevent it, trade-offs, and a "what to build first" checklist. About the author: Sai Prasad Veluru is a Senior Software Engineer at Immihub, where he works on distributed systems and production AI. Over eleven years in the industry — including engineering roles at Apple, JPMorgan Chase, and Visa — he has designed and operated high-throughput ingestion platforms, real-time streaming systems, and cloud-native data infrastructure, and he now builds agentic AI systems engineered to survive production. He is the author of twenty-five publications on distributed systems, stream processing, federated learning, and production AI, cited more than 150 times, and he serves as a judge at HackMIT and MHacks. items.title: Reporting LLM-Assisted Qualitative Data Analysis: Literature-Informed COREQ-AI and SRQR-AI Extensions
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in qualitative data analysis, introducing reporting considerations not explicitly addressed by COREQ or SRQR. This study used a structured literature review–informed methodological synthesis to develop preliminary COREQ-AI and SRQR-AI extensions. Of 2,127 records identified, the synthesis included 65 studies. The proposed extensions address model specification, prompt transparency, algorithmic reflexivity, human-in-the-loop validation, AI auditability, data governance, and ethical accountability. Five independent researchers appraised the extensions; 80% considered them relevant and clear, 100% applicable, and 60% indicated that further refinement was needed. Illustrative applications further demonstrated their potential to identify AI-specific reporting information not captured by the original guidelines. COREQ-AI and SRQR-AI are preliminary, literature-informed reporting extensions intended to improve transparency and critical appraisal of LLM-assisted qualitative analysis; they are not validated or consensus-derived standards. Further empirical evaluation, stakeholder consultation, and consensus development are required.

items.title: Reproducible Software Environments for Hardware-Accelerated Science
items.abstract: Scientific researchers need reproducible software environments for complex applications that can run across heterogeneous computing platforms. Modern open source tools, like Pixi [1], provide automatic reproducibility solutions for all dependencies while providing a high-level interface well suited for researchers. This poster will provide a practical overview of using Pixi to easily create scientific and artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) environments that benefit from hardware acceleration, across multiple machines and platforms. The focus will be on CUDA applications, such as machine learning frameworks, and CUDA-enabled research software [2-4]. As AI/ML becomes a modern part of the scientific toolkit, the need to have robustly reproducible scientific computing environments that support hardware acceleration, e.g. with CUDA, becomes more important. However, historically just installing a working CUDA environment on a single machine, let alone on multiple platforms with different requirements, could be a difficult task for non-experts. This led to many scientific machine learning workflows being reliably runnable on only particular machines, and, even worse, with environments that were not reproducible across time. With significant recent advancements by the NVIDIA open source team and the conda-forge open source community, the entire CUDA stack — from compilers to development libraries — is now distributed on conda-forge. This significantly reduces the overhead to install CUDA dependencies, but packaging and distribution of binaries alone does not solve the problem of reproducibility. With automatic multi-platform digest-level lock file support for all dependencies that are available on package indexes (like PyPI and conda-forge), highly efficient solving strategies, and high-level user interfaces, Pixi provides a missing piece to the scientific researcher toolkit. The technology allows researchers to easily specify the hardware acceleration requirements they have, multiple different computational environments needed for their experiments, and required software dependencies. They can then quickly solve for a multi-platform lock file of all the dependencies required, down to the compiler level. This makes it possible to have multiple hardware-accelerated environments defined that are able to run hardware-accelerated workflows across heterogeneous machines with different GPU types and CUDA compatibility. The poster will also cover practical recommendations for deployment of locked software environments into production computing environments on traditional batch computing systems (e.g. HTCondor, Slurm) as well as cloud-native computing systems (e.g. Kubernetes, commercial cloud instances) [5]. It will also provide examples and links to published resources that provide fully templated Linux container definition files for arbitrary Pixi workspaces and computing requirements.

items.title: Research on AI-Assisted Mathematics Teaching in Primary and Secondary Schools (2022-2026)
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support mathematics teaching, yet research examining its instructional effects and implementation conditions in primary and secondary schools remains fragmented. This study reviewed published research on AI-assisted mathematics teaching between 2022 and 2026. Relevant records were retrieved from the Web of Science database using topic searches for AI and mathematics education. Of 262 initially identified records, 44 studies met the stated inclusion criteria and were included in a thematic synthesis. Three principal research areas emerged: instructional effects, factors influencing effectiveness, and strategies for improvement. The reviewed studies generally reported favourable outcomes for students’ mathematics achievement, conceptual understanding, interest, motivation and classroom engagement, although some interventions produced limited or inconsistent benefits. AI tools also supported teachers’ lesson planning, resource preparation, assessment, learning diagnosis and instructional decision-making. Reported outcomes depended on teacher-related factors, including AI literacy, attitudes and pedagogical competencies; student-related factors, including self-regulation, digital literacy and interaction patterns; technological factors, particularly accuracy, usability and personalisation; and contextual factors, including infrastructure, family support and educational resources. Suggested improvements included professional development, teacher-led implementation, clearer ethical and data-governance arrangements, and the development of more reliable mathematics-specific tools. The findings indicate that AI can provide useful instructional support, but its effectiveness depends on appropriate educational integration and local conditions. Longitudinal classroom research is needed to clarify sustained outcomes and the interaction of these factors.

items.title: Research progress on bowel preparation regimens before colonoscopy: a narrative review
items.abstract: Adequate bowel preparation is the single most important determinant of colonoscopy quality, yet suboptimal preparation affects up to one-quarter of colonoscopies, leading to repeat procedures, increased health-system costs, and health disparities. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence on bowel preparation regimens through a public health lens, organized around four interconnected dimensions: cleansing efficacy, safety, tolerability, and population-specific applicability. We define and classify preparation regimens by volume (high-volume ≥4 L, low-volume 2–<4 L, ultra-low-volume <2 L) and administration schedule (split-dose, same-day). Low-volume, split-dose formulations achieve non-inferior cleansing efficacy to high-volume 4L polyethylene glycol (PEG) regimens, with improved patient tolerability and compliance. The Boston Bowel Preparation Scale (BBPS) is the most widely adopted assessment instrument; commonly used adequate preparation is defined as total BBPS ≥6 with each segment ≥2, although definitions vary across studies. PEG-based preparations maintain the most favorable safety profile, particularly in patients with renal or cardiovascular comorbidities, while sodium phosphate carries a small but clinically significant risk of acute phosphate nephropathy. Special populations—including older adults with frailty and polypharmacy, patients with inflammatory bowel disease, and those with diabetes—require tailored preparation strategies. Emerging evidence on glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), linaclotide, simethicone, dietary optimization, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based bowel preparation assessment is critically evaluated. Health system implications, including the impact of inadequate preparation on resource utilization, adherence barriers linked to health literacy, and equity considerations, are examined. The review concludes that no single regimen is universally optimal; personalized preparation strategies integrating risk stratification, AI-assisted quality assessment, and evidence-based adjunctive protocols represent the most promising path toward improving colonoscopy outcomes at the population level.

items.title: Research progress on the application of multi-scale computational methods in the research and development of anti-tuberculosis infection drugs
items.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), driven by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), remains a leading cause of mortality from infectious disease worldwide.​ The global dissemination of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains—coupled with protracted treatment regimens and the persistence of latent infection—has not only compromised first-line chemotherapies but also underscored the stagnation of conventional drug development pipelines. In this review, we systematically synthesize how multi-scale computational strategies are reshaping anti-TB drug discovery and explicitly delineate their hierarchical integration—a cohesive framework that, to our knowledge, has yet to be comprehensively mapped in the existing literature.​ We survey four interconnected computational layers: (i) systems and network pharmacology for macroscopic target and pathway prioritization; (ii) machine learning (ML) for mesoscopic virtual screening, resistance classification, and ADMET prediction; (iii) molecular docking for microscopic elucidation of ligand–target binding modes; and (iv) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations for atomic-level validation of binding poses and assessment of complex stability. Representative studies demonstrate that this workflow has pinpointed pivotal TB vulnerabilities (e.g., MmpL3, InhA, DprE1, ATP synthase, and FtsZ), enabled ML models to predict drug resistance from genomic data with high fidelity, and identified promising candidates such as vazabitide A (predicted binding affinity of −85.8 kcal/mol against Pks13) alongside repurposed agents (e.g., aldoxorubicin, quarfloxin). Critically, these computational predictions are reinforced by orthogonal experimental validation spanning in vitro enzymatic and phenotypic assays, in vivo infection models, clinical pharmacokinetic profiling, and multi-omics corroboration. We conclude that the top-down pipeline-spanning network pharmacology to ML, docking, and MD-integrated with bottom-up feedback constitutes a closed-loop paradigm that accelerates lead identification while addressing emergent drug resistance.​ Nevertheless, inherent limitations in predictive reliability and cross-layer error propagation necessitate rigorous downstream experimental validation. Looking forward, generative artificial intelligence, self-driving laboratories, and standardized cross-method benchmarking are poised to consolidate this multi-scale pipeline into a robust engine for next-generation anti-TB therapeutics.

items.title: Resident resource use in clinical settings: an institutional survey
items.abstract: Background: We explored which point of care (POC) resources medical residents at the University at Buffalo use in clinical settings. We specifically sought to gather feedback from residents who help train medical students to see how they discover, use, and promote resources to support patient care. Case Presentation: We developed an eight question Qualtrics survey. Residency program coordinators emailed the survey to approximately 445 residents in the following programs: Family Medicine, Internal Medicine, Combined Internal Medicine and Pediatrics, Neurology, Child Neurology, Obstetrics and Gynecology, Pediatrics, Psychiatry, Surgery, Plastic Surgery, and Vascular Surgery. The programs we targeted all correspond to required clerkship rotations. The survey was open for two weeks in June 2025. Thirty-nine residents (8.8%) completed our survey. Thirty-five, or nearly 90% of respondents, reported that they frequently use UpToDate, followed by twenty-three (59.0%) that use OpenEvidence, and seventeen that use MDCalc (43.6%). The residents we surveyed were inclined to recommend similar resources to medical students. They most often hear about new resources from other residents and attendings, via announcements on social media or podcasts, or by attending grand rounds and conferences. Conclusions: Our results highlight the continued popularity of UpToDate among medical trainees but also suggest that residents frequently use OpenEvidence in clinical settings. Further studies are needed to determine the impact of artificial intelligence tools on patient care and learning outcomes.
