items.title: Responsible and Trustworthy Agentic AI: Governance, Assurance, Explainability, Controllability, and Human Oversight: A Comprehensive Survey
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence combines goal-directed reasoning, planning, memory, tool use, adaptation and multi-agent coordination with the ability to affect external systems. This capability raises problems of authorization, safety, human oversight, accountability and the evidence required to justify reliance. This non-systematic integrative survey distinguishes AI ethics, responsible AI, governance, trustworthiness, assurance, explainability, security and controllability; synthesizes preventive, detective, corrective, human-based and agent-based controls; and compares responsibility and oversight arrangements across the agent lifecycle. Building on established governance and meaningful-human-control research, it proposes an authority-control-assurance-accountability mapping that connects normative requirements to delegated decision rights, enforceable controls, observable evidence, escalation conditions and identifiable organizational owners. Two fictional cases illustrate the proposed mapping for document access and software changes. The framework is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirically validated assurance standard. The survey identifies limitations of supervisory-agent independence, long-horizon explanation, dynamic authorization and continuous re-assurance, and specifies research questions for future evaluation.

items.title: Retrieve What Helps, Only When It Helps: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Machine Translation
items.abstract: Retrieving external knowledge can improve large language model (LLM) translation by providing supplementary information such as idiom interpretations and terminology. However, existing retrieval-augmented machine translation systems typically apply predefined retrieval strategies uniformly across all inputs. We argue that translation operates in a partial-evidence regime: LLM's parametric knowledge suffices for many inputs, while external evidence benefits a subset and usually supports rather than directly provides the desired translation. This creates two challenges: deciding when to retrieve and what evidence to acquire. We introduce Selective Retrieval-Augmented Translation (SRAT), an agentic reinforcement learning framework that learns when to translate directly or retrieve, what to retrieve, and how to integrate these decisions by optimizing final translation quality. To align evidence retrieval with downstream translation quality rather than simple semantic similarity, we further develop joint Plackett--Luce optimization and translation-quality contrastive training for retriever-training. Experiments on idiom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation with offline or online retrieval show that SRAT consistently outperforms never- and always-retrieve baselines, and quality-aligned retriever training provides further gains when similarity-based retrieval is insufficient. The results demonstrate the benefit of treating retrieval as a learnable translation action rather than fixed preprocessing.

items.title: Review on unobtrusive estimation of team processes underlying team situation awareness: shared mental models and team coordination
items.abstract: Introduction Team situation awareness (SA) is essential for effective team performance. Yet, current methods rely on potentially biased self-reports and obtrusive tools such as task probes. Objective, unobtrusive, and continuous methods for monitoring team SA could support its improvement. In contrast to individual SA, unobtrusive measures of team SA have not been systematically reviewed. Because team SA is an umbrella concept, we adapted a framework proposed by Salmon et al., identifying two components that can potentially be measured unobtrusively: shared mental models (SMMs) and team coordination. This systematic review examines behavioural and physiological technologies that may enable unobtrusive measurement of these components. Methods We conducted a systematic literature review of studies investigating behavioural technologies, such as verbal communication and eye-tracking, and physiological technologies, such as electroencephalography, for unobtrusive measurement of team SMMs and coordination. We searched Web of Science (May and July 2025) for relevant literature published between 2000 and 2025. We included peer-reviewed articles published in English. In total, 19 studies addressing team SMMs and 33 addressing team coordination were included. We extracted sample and team size, task environment, operationalisation of team SMMs and coordination, and their relationship with unobtrusive measures. Results Cardiac measures (42%) and verbal communication (47%) were most popular for estimating team SMMs, while functional near-infrared spectroscopy (27%) and cardiac measures (30%) were most popular for estimating team coordination. Interpersonal synchrony—the temporal contiguity and interdependence of physiological and/or behavioural activity between teammates—was applied in 70% of team coordination studies. Studies covered diverse tasks and settings, from laboratory-based cognitive tasks and controlled physical tasks to real-world environments, including surgery. Various methods were used to operationalise SMMs and coordination, including participant experience, expert assessment, and self-reports. Discussion Findings suggest that team SMMs and coordination cannot be measured as single, unified constructs using one unobtrusive measure. Instead, different measures may provide information about specific aspects of these processes. Future research should begin with task analysis to identify relevant aspects of team SA and derive appropriate measures for the specific task environment. Task-related behavioural actions also represent a potentially valuable, yet often overlooked, category of unobtrusive measures. A key limitation is the substantial variation in how SMMs and coordination were operationalised and measured, making direct comparisons difficult. Future work should investigate how identified measures relate directly to team SA using validated measures.

items.title: Rice Water Depth Estimation Using Machine Learning and Multi-Modal Remote Sensing in Semi-Arid Australia
items.abstract: Water is crucial for rice growth, particularly in semi-arid Australia, where climate change threatens water allocation for rice growers and challenges the sustainability of the rice industry. Estimating water depth using remote sensing can be beneficial, as it can help growers transition from traditional continuous flooding (CF) to irrigation practices such as Delayed Permanent Water (DPW) and Aerobic Rice (AR), which are promising pathways to ensure industry sustainability. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) has been widely evaluated for water depth prediction in rice crops. To date, a significant gap remains in the performance of the proposed models, with authors suggesting the use of optical and SAR data to improve their estimates. To this end, this research evaluated three machine learning (ML) models to estimate water depth in rice under different irrigation practices in the Australian semi-arid region. Three different ML approaches (Tree-based, Neural Networks, and pretrained foundational model) were evaluated with three data configurations: Set 1 with SAR only, set 2 with Optical Only, and Set 3 with multimodal (SAR and Optical) data. The pre-trained foundational model achieved the best results, with RMSE of 14.19 cm, MAE of 10.01 cm, R2 of 0.63, KGE of 0.73, and CCC of 0.78. items.title: Risk prediction models for macrovascular complications in type 2 diabetes mellitus: from traditional risk scores to multimodal intelligent prediction
items.abstract: Macrovascular complications are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Early risk identification and accurate risk stratification are essential for both primary and secondary cardiovascular prevention. With the rapid development of electronic health records, medical imaging, multi-omics technologies, and artificial intelligence (AI), risk prediction models for diabetic macrovascular complications have evolved from traditional statistical approaches to machine learning-, deep learning-, and multimodal AI-driven models. However, despite substantial improvements in predictive performance, current models remain limited by heterogeneous target populations, inconsistent outcome definitions, insufficient external validation, limited clinical interpretability, and inadequate real-world implementation, thereby restricting their clinical translation. This review summarizes the evolution, data sources, modeling methodologies, clinical applications, and future perspectives of risk prediction models for macrovascular complications in T2DM. We first describe the transition from conventional cardiovascular risk scores, including the Framingham Risk Score, to diabetes-specific models such as the UKPDS Risk Engine, ADVANCE, RECODe, and SCORE2-Diabetes, followed by the emergence of AI-based prediction models. We then review the major data sources used in contemporary prediction models, including clinical characteristics, laboratory biomarkers, vascular function and imaging, multi-omics profiles, and wearable device-derived data. Furthermore, we compare the strengths and limitations of traditional statistical methods, machine learning, deep learning, and multitask learning with respect to predictive performance, interpretability, and clinical applicability, and discuss the major challenges related to study design, external validation, data quality, algorithmic bias, and real-world implementation. Finally, we propose that future risk prediction models for diabetic macrovascular complications will evolve from single-source data to multimodal data integration, from static risk estimation to dynamic risk trajectories, from single outcomes to multiple interconnected cardiovascular outcomes, from prognosis prediction to individualized treatment benefit prediction, and from standalone algorithms to continuously learning clinical decision support systems. Emerging technologies, including foundation models, large language models, digital twins, causal inference, and continuous learning frameworks, are expected to drive the transition from Risk Prediction to Clinical Decision and ultimately Patient Benefit, thereby advancing precision prevention and individualized management of diabetes.

items.title: Role of Construction Management in Smart City Infrastructure Development: A Review of Digital Tools, Lean–Sustainable Practices and Implementation Challenges with Evidence from Sagar Smart City, India
items.abstract: The current pace of urbanization has imposed unprecedented strains on transport, water, energy and housing networks and the smart city paradigm has become the key policy response. However, the effectiveness of smart city programmes rely more on the construction management (CM) systems involved in planning, coordination and delivery of the physical infrastructure underpinning smart city programmes. The literature reviewed in the following paper is divided into six themes: smart city concept and smart city components; core functions of CM (planning, scheduling, cost, quality and safety); digital tools (Building Information Modelling (BIM), Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI)); lean and sustainable construction; risk management, stakeholder management, public–private partnership (PPP); and field evidence from smart city Sagar, Madhya Pradesh. The results of the synthesis indicate that the use of BIM-based coordination in the project reduced the number of design errors from 25 to 8 and rework cost by 64%, while lean JIT delivery reduced material waste by 60-67% and smart building systems reduced the energy demand by 40%. The adaptive traffic control in Sagar reduced junction delay by 37.5 %; sensorbased LED street lighting reduced connected load by 52 % and the Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC) reduced complaint response by 75 %. Financial risk (20/25) and inter-agency coordination (20/25) were identified as the main barriers. A challenge–strategy framework and an agenda of future research are suggested on digital twins, AI-assisted scheduling and capacity building.
